However, if you’re running this inside a normal Unix/Linux/macOS shell (or even Windows PowerShell / WSL), you can quickly pull up all files whose names include **“test”** with one of the following commands: | Shell | Command | What it prints | |-------|---------|----------------| | Bash/Zsh/PowerShell (Unix) | ```bash
find . -type f -iname '*test*'
``` | Every regular file under the current directory tree whose filename contains *test*, case‑insensitive. | | Bash/Zsh | ```bash
git ls-files --others --exclude-standard | grep -i test
``` | All tracked/untracked Git files that match *test*. Useful if you’re inside a repo. | | PowerShell | ```powershell
Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File | Where-Object { $_.Name -match '(?i)test' }
``` | Same idea on Windows. | If you prefer a quick visual check without recursion, you can also open a terminal window and type: ``` $ ls | grep -i test ``` That lists only the items immediately in the current directory. --- ### How to integrate this into a script Suppose you’d like to capture the results into a text file called `test_files.txt`. Here’s a tiny snippet you can drop into a bash script: ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash set -o pipefail # Find all files named with “test”, ignore case, and save the full paths: find . -type f -iname "*test*" > test_files.txt echo "Found $(wc -l < test_files.txt) matches." cat test_files.txt # optional preview ``` Run it with: ```bash chmod +x find_test.sh && ./find_test.sh ``` Now you’ll have a ready reference (`test_files.txt`) you can feed into other tooling—copy, delete, archive, whatever you need next. message.content:
Sure thing! Below is a minimal set of shell commands you can paste straight into your terminal (Linux/macOS/Bash or WSL). They’ll:

1. Make sure a folder called **`backup_tests`** exists in the current directory.  
2. Locate every JPEG/PNG/GIF image *and* every plain‑text file whose name includes “test” (case‑insensitive).  
3. Copy those files over to `backup_tests`, preserving the original filenames.

```bash
# 1️⃣ Ensure the target folder exists
mkdir -p backup_tests          # creates it if missing, otherwise does nothing

# 2️⃣ & 3️⃣ Find & copy the desired files
#   • Images – jpeg/jpg/png/gif
#   • Texts – txt
#   • Only copies the file itself (no directory hierarchy)
for ext in jpg jpeg png gif txt ; do \
    find . -maxdepth 1 -type f -iname "*test.*.$ext" -exec cp "{}" backup_tests/ \;
done
```

**What happens**

| Step | Explanation |
|------|-------------|
| `mkdir -p backup_tests` | Creates the folder once; safe to rerun. |
| `find . -maxdepth 1 …` | Looks only in the current directory (not recursing deeper). Adjust `-maxdepth` if you want to dive into subfolders. |
| `-iname "*test.*.$ext"` | Matches any filename that contains “test” anywhere, ignoring case, followed by a dot and the chosen extension. |
| `-exec cp "{}" backup_tests/ \;` | Copies each hit straight into `backup_tests`.

---

### Want to keep the original directory layout?

If you prefer to maintain the folder structure instead of flattening everything into one folder, replace the `cp` line with:

```bash
rsync -R "$PWD"/{}/ backup_tests/
```

(Or simply use `cp --parents`). That keeps nested folders intact while still backing up only the selected files.

Happy shooting—and happy archiving! Let me know if you'd rather see a different approach (like using `tar`, `zip`, or scripting in Python).
